rules.name: is_style_colocated
rules.instructions: Does this stylesheet style COMPONENT behavior via global selectors? Component behavior (hover/active/disabled/selected states; presentation of buttons, rows, triggers) must be styled at the component (Tailwind classes on the element). Global element or attribute selectors - button:not(:disabled), [data-slot=...], .component-class rules that set behavior states - are a second style authority and a violation. NOT violations: @theme token definitions (palette, spacing), base document styles (body, html), non-behavioral resets, and theme assignments to vendor token classes (.hljs-comment etc.).

criteria.true: The file contains at least one global element/attribute selector that styles component behavior (e.g. button:not(:disabled), [data-slot="button"], a .component class setting hover/selected/active states).
criteria.false: No such selector: only @theme tokens, base document styles, non-behavioral resets, and vendor-class theme assignments.

rules.name: is_literal_shared
rules.instructions: This unit is a source file. This file might contain literal values (string, number, etc) carrying the same value at two or more separate places. A shared value should be written once as a named constant in this file and referenced at each place: an identical raw literal at distinct sites is drift waiting to happen.
criteria: No raw literal flows between sites: every repeated literal is either a named constant carried to all its sites, or a per-site use of a shared vocabulary - a styling class string, a prop or option value, an event, sort-key or mode name, a typeof guard comparison string, an error-code name - where each site names the convention. Brevity of a literal alone is not a defect; imports and identifiers are not literals.

Repeated literals are convention vocabulary or typeof guards, however numerous; at most one or two are ambiguous - plausibly a convention, plausibly one value flowing between sites that wants a constant.

At least one literal value appears as the same raw literal in two or more distinct places where the sites share that value, and no single named constant in this file carries it to all of them. Convention words do not count even when numerous: typeof guard strings, styling classes, prop/event/mode names, error-code names - those are per-site uses of a vocabulary, not a value flowing.
Pervasive: multiple distinct values repeat as raw literals across their sites with no constants, so several renames would miss sites.

rules.name: is_value_tokenized
rules.instructions: In this stylesheet, sharing wants a token: a value that serves the same purpose at two or more places should be written once as a custom property or @theme token and referenced at each use. Coincidental equality is not sharing: distinct roles each declaring their value inline, even when the literals match, are separate declarations - do not count them and do not merge roles into one token to satisfy this rule. Judge what is observable: raw literals at USE sites (selectors, utilities, rules) that repeat a value instead of referencing the token that already carries it. @font-face descriptors are exempt: CSS forbids var() inside them.

criteria.true: At least one raw literal appears at two or more use sites serving the same purpose - a selector, utility class, or rule repeating a value that a custom property or @theme token in this file already carries or should carry - instead of referencing that token.
criteria.false: Every value serving the same purpose at multiple places is declared once as a token and referenced at its uses; declarations of distinct roles may hold equal literals - that is coincidental, not sharing.

rules.name: is_token_role_separated
rules.instructions: In a stylesheet, a custom property names a semantic role - gutter, cell padding, caption line-height, page background - not a value. Two roles whose values coincide today must still own separate custom properties: aliasing one to another by coincidental value couples them, so changing one role silently moves the other. Equal values are not equal semantics. Judge the FILE: does any custom property alias a different role's token, or does one token serve clearly different roles at its use sites? Same-role aliases are by design, not defects: theme variants (.dark re-declaring the same token) and fallback chains var(--a, --b) re-using the same role.

criteria.true: At least one token couples distinct semantic roles: a custom property defined as a reference to another token whose name denotes a different role, or one token consumed by use sites of clearly different roles.
criteria.false: Every custom property names exactly one role: aliases exist only between same-role names (theme-variant re-declarations), and value equality between different roles stays as separate literal definitions.

rules.name: is_token_role_declared
rules.instructions: A design token declares a role: the name states what it is for, the value inline states what it carries (--background: #fafafa). Judge this stylesheet's token declarations and their comments. Comments that only separate or label groups are fine. A comment that explains a token's meaning or visualizes its value is a patch: the declaration could carry that meaning itself.
criteria: Every token declares a role with its value inline; comments only separate or label groups - or there are no comments.
One or two comments explain a token's meaning or visualize its value; the declarations could carry it themselves.
A palette of scale-named constants (shade or color names) sits behind role tokens through var() chains, and comments routinely bridge the gap the indirection opens.
Comments are load-bearing documentation of the token system: meaning and values live in prose - histories, ratios, provenance - not in the declarations.
